### Title
ReDoS in `isValidEmail` email-address regex reachable via `uri.js` payment-request parsing - (File: validation_utils.js)

### Summary
`validation_utils.js` implements `isValidEmail()` using a hand-written regex with nested unbounded quantifiers of the classic `(x+(\.x+)*)` "evil regex" shape known to be vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking (the same bug class as CVE-2021-43307's `semver-regex` ReDoS). This function is invoked from `uri.js`'s `parseUri()` when parsing a `byteball:`/`obyte:` payment-request URI's address component, which can originate from data an unprivileged party controls (a URI/QR string, a pasted payment link, or a chat/contact message that gets parsed as a request). [1](#0-0) 

### Finding Description
The regex is:
```
/^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/
```
The local-part alternative `([^...]+(\.[^...]+)*)` contains a repeated group whose inner character class overlaps with itself across iterations, allowing exponential backtracking when the input contains a long run of matching characters followed by a character that forces the overall match to fail (e.g. no `@`, or a bad domain). This is structurally the same class of bug flagged in the external report for `semver-regex`: an attacker-controlled string fed into `.test()` triggers exponential-time matching on carefully crafted, otherwise-invalid input. [2](#0-1) 

`isValidEmail` is called from `uri.js` while parsing the `address` part of a `byteball:`/`obyte:` URI (used for payment requests, e.g. scanned QR codes or pasted links): [3](#0-2) 

`parseUri` treats the main part of the URI as a candidate address, and falls through to `isValidEmail(address)` if it's not a valid Obyte address, before other lighter checks (`steem/`, `reddit/`, phone regex). Because the email-shaped alternative is checked first and is unbounded in length, an attacker can construct a URI whose address portion is a long string of otherwise-legal local-part characters (no `@`, or a malformed domain) to force worst-case backtracking in the wallet/UI code that parses incoming payment-request URIs.

### Impact Explanation
This is a synchronous, CPU-bound regex evaluation. A crafted payment-request URI/string that gets parsed via `parseUri` can block the event loop of the node/wallet process that parses it, causing a local denial of service (the process becomes unresponsive while validating/relaying units, syncing the DAG, or servicing other wallets) for as long as the pathological match takes, which grows exponentially with input length. This matches the "network unable to confirm new units" impact bucket if the affected process is a full node/hub that parses user/URI-supplied strings while otherwise participating in unit validation and confirmation flows.

### Likelihood Explanation
Likelihood is moderate: the attack requires the victim (or their software) to call `parseUri()` on an attacker-supplied string, which happens naturally for wallets/nodes that accept `byteball:`/`obyte:` links (e.g., from a chat partner, contact request, or scanned QR). No cryptographic material or privileged position is required — any counterparty who can send a link/string to be parsed can trigger it.

### Recommendation
Replace the vulnerable email regex in `validation_utils.js`'s `isValidEmail` with a non-backtracking implementation (e.g., a linear-time email format check, or a well-vetted RFC 5322-lite regex without nested unbounded quantifiers over overlapping character classes), and/or impose a maximum input length before running the regex in both `isValidEmail` and its call site in `uri.js`.
